Sparse

/SPARS/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Sparse means thinly scattered or spread out, with wide gaps in between — not dense or crowded.

Sparse means thinly scattered or spread out, with wide gaps in between — not dense or crowded. His notes for the exam were sparse: a few scattered phrases on an otherwise empty page.

Worked Example

The sparse audience left whole rows of seats empty, so the comedian invited everyone to move down to the front.

Sparse describes how thinly the people were spread across the theater — a few here and there with big gaps between them. It says nothing about the show's quality, only about spacing and density.

How Sparse Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

scattered

scattered: spread thinly over an area

patchy

patchy: uneven, with bare gaps

thin

thin: not densely packed

Antonyms

dense

dense: tightly packed together

lush

lush: growing thickly and richly

How Strong Is It? — thin → sparse → barren

thin vs. sparse

thin vs. sparse: "Thin" is milder than sparse — a thin crowd still fills most of the space, just loosely.

barren vs. sparse

barren vs. sparse: "Barren" is stronger than sparse — a sparse field has a little growing here and there, but a barren field has almost nothing at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — sparse

Root — sparse: from Latin sparsus, past participle of spargere, 'to scatter, strew'

Put it together

Put it together: Sparse comes straight from Latin spargere, 'to scatter' — something sparse looks as if it was scattered by hand, a little landing here and a little there, with empty space between.

Use the root in a new word: disperse

Use the root in a new word: disperse: When the rain started, the crowd began to disperse, scattering in every direction to find shelter.

Root Check

Word Choice

Neutral / descriptive

Sparse is about physical spacing — sparse hair, sparse vegetation, a sparse crowd all have visible gaps. Its neighbor in this unit, scarce, is different: scarce means the supply isn't enough for the demand. A desert's plants are sparse (spread thin); its water is scarce (not enough to go around).
